webTitle: How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all | Jonathan Freedland

fields.headline: How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all
fields.trailText: Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
fields.bodyText: What is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’s controlled by a secret cabal of its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for which the first postal ballots were sent out today. That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage. At the centre of it is the single act that is already defining Trump’s second term: his reckless, failed war of choice against Iran. No matter how many times he declares mission accomplished or claims to have destroyed the Iranian military or to have reopened the strait of Hormuz, the facts keep telling a different story. In the past week, the two sides shifted from an economic standoff back to a shooting war, with the US firing on Iranian targets that included a wedding party, killing four, and Tehran striking out all over the neighbourhood, hitting Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain. The impact on US voters is severe, felt most directly through rising petrol prices and grocery bills. But look at the graph measuring the cost the US government must pay to borrow money: it’s been a steep upward climb since 28 February, the day the war began, hitting a fresh high on Tuesday. For consumers, that rise translates into an expected jump in interest rates. It means that many of those casting ballots are likely to be doing so just as they start paying more on their credit card bills and mortgages. Given that Trump was elected in November 2024 on a promise to bring down inflation, it’s hard to think of a worse environment for a governing party about to face the voters’ verdict. And that’s before you consider the disenchantment of the Maga faithful, who thought the whole point of Trump was an end to forever wars in the Middle East. And yet, Iran may not even be the most electorally damaging of Trump’s foreign adventures. He is, and it would once have been absurd to write this sentence, leading his country into a state of war with … Canada. It’s easy to laugh at the petty gestures, such as Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move shamefully followed, and therefore endorsed, by Apple and Google in their map apps. But the economic confrontation is serious – and seriously damaging to Republicans’ electoral prospects. For which US states are hit hardest by Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s tariffs? Why, it’s Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Texas, all of which just happen to have key senate contests this year. Republican candidates in those states now have to explain why a crucial and previously friendly export market – Canada takes nearly a third of Iowa’s exports, for example – has suddenly turned icy. What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot. Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, with seven in 10 Americans saying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans, there is deep concern over their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters. So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too. It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whether demolishing the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly. And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas was impeached by his fellow Republicans on a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even that red-state stronghold is shaky. Put it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance? One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime. But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new book Regime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

webTitle: North Carolina becomes first state to send out mail-in ballots for US midterms

fields.headline: North Carolina becomes first state to send out mail-in ballots for US midterms
fields.trailText: State decides to proceed hours after Trump administration asks supreme court to let it carry out proposed crackdown
fields.bodyText: North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for November’s US midterm elections on Friday, as Donald Trump’s administration fights to impose sweeping restrictions on the practice before millions of Americans cast their votes. The state’s decision to proceed – hours after Trump’s officials asked the supreme court to let the administration press ahead with its proposed crackdown – comes amid deep uncertainty over whether new federal rules governing mail ballots will be allowed to take effect, and whether the US Postal Service can implement the changes in time. North Carolina is first out of the gate because its state statute requires county boards to begin sending absentee ballots 60 days before a general election – one of the earliest start dates in the country. Other states set their own timelines, ranging from a few weeks before election day to, in a handful of cases, similarly early starts, meaning most will follow in the coming days and weeks. The Trump administration asked the supreme court on Thursday to let it revive a rule barring the postal service from delivering ballots in states that don’t share voter data with the federal government, and requiring ballot envelopes to be screened against new standards before delivery. D John Sauer, the US solicitor general, told the justices that a lower court’s freeze on the plan was causing “serious irreparable harm” to the government, states and voters. It is the second time in weeks the administration has turned to the court over the plan, part of an executive order Trump signed in March directing agencies to compile citizen lists for use in screening mail ballots. A federal judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, blocked the plan in June, ruling that it encroached on states’ constitutional authority over elections. The supreme court’s conservative majority sided with Trump in August but called the challenge premature, leaving the door open for further litigation once the plan was finalized. Talwani froze key parts of it again on 27 August. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who oversees emergency applications from the region, has not granted the administration’s request for an immediate stay. Instead, she has given challengers until Tuesday to respond, a timeline that leaves little room for the postal service to act before ballots need to be in voters’ hands nationwide. Underscoring how tight the window has become with barely two months left before polls open, a postal service official told the Massachusetts court this week that the agency was still refining its screening system and expected to make it available to states on a voluntary basis “sometime next week”.

webTitle: Private equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile up

fields.headline: Private equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile up
fields.trailText: Private equity firms and the companies they own employ over 13 million, from startups to rural hospitals and large retailers, but experts’ concerns of collapse are growing
fields.bodyText: Retail stalwarts Saks and Eddie Bauer filed for bankruptcy. Kmart and JoAnn Fabrics are gone for good, a trail of layoffs and disappointed customers in their wake. Hospital giant Steward Health Care collapsed, costing thousands of jobs and leaving several communities without a local hospital. These once-trusted US companies have one thing in common: they were owned by private equity investors, who load companies with debt when they buy them and squeeze out profits as they restructure. The business model is now facing an existential crisis that may have profound ramifications across the US. Once fringe financial players, private equity investors have bought up vast swathes of US, UK, European and Australian industry, from local dentists to shopping mall anchors and fast-food chains and even the video games company EA. In the US, these firms and the companies they own, employ more than 13 million people in everything from quirky startups like Dave’s Hot Chicken, Two Men and a Truck and School of Rock (all owned by Roark Capital) to the US’s largest pet retailer PetSmart (BC Partners) and classics Birkenstock (purchased by L Catterton in 2021) and Pyrex (owned by Centre Lane Partners). Private equity investors also bought thousands of healthcare facilities in the US in recent years, including non-profit hospice care, rural hospitals and small-town dentists’ offices. But this wave of buyouts is running smack into a wall of persistently high interest rates, rising buyout prices and pressure over moribund returns. Private equity funds are sitting on a “record number of unsold companies, many of which they’ve been unable to sell … or at least unable to sell at the prices that they’re looking for”, said Jim Baker, the executive director of the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, an industry watchdog. The US’s over 13,500 unsold companies in private equity portfolios include 2,563 consumer products and services companies, PitchBook data shows, and 1,536 healthcare companies. Hundreds of these have been sitting in PE portfolios for years longer than funds historically like to keep their investments. A growing concern is that “eventually, the companies that have accumulated this much debt are going to collapse”, said Audrey Stienon, Industrial Policy Program Manager at Open Markets, an anti-monopoly thinktank that is examining private equity’s role in the greater economy. And often, what private equity buys up “are really, really important businesses”, Stienon said, providing jobs or vital services to local communities. “When they go down, either you need to bail them out, or you need to find someone to save them, or else you’re just stuck with fewer options for consumers down the line.” Executives in the industry argue their deep pockets will help businesses weather any upcoming crisis. “Private equity-backed businesses face the same higher interest rates and economic pressures as other companies, but they also have committed investment partners that can provide additional capital and keep investing through difficult periods,” Will Dunham, the president and CEO of American Investment Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement. “Ultimately, private equity only succeeds when the businesses it invests in succeed over the long term,” he said. High rates, more competition Think of private equity deals like buying a home, explains Brad Lipton, director of corporate power and financial regulation at the Roosevelt Institute. Investors buy the company with a hefty loan, like a mortgage, but plan to sell in a matter of years. But unlike with a mortgage, the company is on the hook for making payments, not the buyer, and the buyer almost always plans to sell in a few years. “Interest rates being unexpectedly high may have complicated exit strategies,” Lipton said. Private equity firms promise investors higher returns than the stock market, in exchange for holding on to their money for a longer time period, generally 10 years, a business model that’s been the same for decades. “What has changed is that the price of buying a target company has gone through the roof,” as the number of private equity funds increased, explains Rosemary Batt, a Cornell University management and labor professor who studies the industry’s impacts on workers and companies. Healthcare companies that once sold at 11 times EBITDA, a measure of enterprise value, are now priced at 18 times or more, for example. That makes exiting the investment for a profit even more difficult on investors – and on customers and employees. The higher prices for buyouts are “putting even more pressure on PE firms to squeeze the juice out of their portfolio companies”, Batt said, at a time when there’s almost no regulation governing how they do that. “They can engage in financial engineering or just slash and burn on the operating side,” Batt said. “And it takes years for anyone to really see it.” As they hold the company, these investors generally channel free cashflow to “creditors and equityholders, often constraining capital expenditures, worker training, and safety investments”, the University of Chicago’s Business Law Review warns. Tightening macroeconomic conditions can result in forced restructurings “that are costly and value‑destroying for the going concern”. One vulnerable area is rural hospitals and other health provider chains which could face cashflow issues, making debt payments even more difficult, as the Trump administration’s cuts to the Affordable Care Act tax credits and Medicaid bite, warns Pablo Willis, spokesman for the Americans for Tax Fairness, which is advocating for changes to how private equity managers compensation and the firms overall are taxed. “There’s bound to be a very negative effect,” he said. A lack of financial transparency means it is hard to predict where or when, though. Companies owned by private equity generally don’t disclose their debt levels or other financials unless they go public or issue bonds themselves. “By design, the industry takes place in the shadows,” Lipton said, so “everything has to begin with the thought that we don’t have a lot of clarity.” More bankruptcies ahead In a hint of the turmoil to come, private equity-backed companies have accounted for the lion’s share of big corporate bankruptcies in 2025 and the first half of 2026, research from the Private Equity Stakeholder Project shows. The biggest determinant of whether or not a company will go bankrupt is leverage – the amount of borrowed money explains Edith Hotchkiss, a finance professor at Boston College. Private equity-backed companies are no more likely to default than other similarly leveraged firms, but their business models mean they have more debt. They carry debt of about 50% of their enterprise value, recent studies show. US consumers have felt private equity’s impact through the deteriorating quality of some fast-food outlets and disappearing stores as brands under PE ownership go broke. Other industries have been hit too. More than 60% of big manufacturing bankruptcies in the US last year were private equity-backed, Baker said, as were an outsized number of healthcare bankruptcies. Still, the number of PE-backed companies entering bankruptcy declined in 2025 from the year before, even as overall bankruptcies climbed, S&P found, as more companies pursued out-of-court settlements. The entire process is disruptive by nature. “By definition there is not enough money to go around to pay” a company’s debts, Roosevelt’s Lipton said. “Someone is going to lose out and all too often that can be workers” who are owed pensions. “It is a cause of concern for workers and consumers left holding the bag,” said Lipton. New rules ahead Private equity operates without the rules and regulatory oversight of publicly traded companies. The industry has long argued that because it caters to sophisticated, high-net worth investors, it doesn’t need the same scrutiny. But tens of thousands of layoffs, high bankruptcy rates, and the soaring wealth of dozens of private equity billionaires has created bipartisan momentum for more oversight, even before the current interest rate crisis. And Donald Trump’s push to allow everyday Americans to invest in the sector through their retirement plans has raised new concerns. Congress’s June housing bill curbs private equity investments in single-family homes. November’s midterm elections, which are widely expected to deliver one or both houses of Congress to Democrats, could see a sea change for the industry in Washington, while several states are pursuing their own regulation. “For private equity, the question increasingly is not whether Congress will investigate private equity firms and their practices, but rather where the scrutiny will turn to next,” corporate law firm Holland and Knight warned this month. Multiple bills are circulating on Capitol Hill that would regulate how private equity is taxed, how it can invest in certain industries and how fund managers and investors can take profits. States’ bills would limit private equity in healthcare, scrutinize deals more closely and put caps on debt. The “Let Kids Play” Act seeks to ban private equity from youth community sports, now a “$40bn industry dominated by private equity, with the singular goal of extracting as much profit as possible from families”, it contends. The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, one of the industry’s most vocal critics in Washington, is leading a healthcare bill that seeks criminal penalties for “executives who loot health care entities like nursing homes and hospitals if that looting results in a patient’s death” and clawbacks of PE compensation. Whether US consumers see some relief could depend on what state they live in, or what other issues Congress takes up in the fall. “Even Democrats will be very hard pressed to do much,” if they have any clout in Congress, Batt predicts, because they have so much on their plate. “The best opportunities right now are for local and state level initiatives,” she said.

webTitle: Trump administration asks supreme court to intervene over judge’s ban on USPS mail-in voting restrictions – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump administration asks supreme court to intervene over judge’s ban on USPS mail-in voting restrictions – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: We’re wrapping up our live coverage for the day. Here are today’s key developments in US politics: The Trump administration filed an emergency request asking the US supreme court to lift order blocking USPS from implementing mail-in voting restrictions. Chuck Schumer said the president was “[attempting] to destroy the integrity of our elections” with the move. Excavation work on Donald Trump’s “Great Triumphal Arch” project in Washington is set to begin in the coming weeks, interior secretary Doug Burgum said. Congressman Don Beyer, whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery, described the arch project as “illegal, gridlock-increasing [and] narcissistic”. Missouri’s supreme court ruled that a Donald Trump-backed US House map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, preventing it from being used in the upcoming November election. Trump and Republicans fumed over the decision. Maryland’s supreme court has decided that a Democrat-backed congressional redistricting amendment can go before voters in the state in November in a win for Democrats. Donald Trump announced an interim replacement for army secretary, Dan Driscoll, who suddenly resigned earlier this week amid reports of tension between him and defense secretary Pete Hegseth. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass has been asked to testify before a congressional subcommittee as part of an investigation into the “potential misallocation” of federal funds by the region’s Homeless Services Authority. Congressman Robert Garcia described the move as “another attempt by Donald Trump and House Republicans to launch a witch hunt against Mayor Karen Bass and Los Angeles.” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass has been asked to testify before a congressional subcommittee as part of an investigation into the “potential misallocation” of federal funds by the region’s Homeless Services Authority. The Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency said in a letter to Bass that it was looking at “waste, fraud, and abuse” of federal grants to address homelessness. Federal officials are investigating the agency’s use of funds because of “repeated false statements and its irresponsible actions and failures, including its lack of financial management, internal controls, and safeguards against conflicts of interest,” the letter states. The Trump administration sought to freeze funding for the agency earlier this year – a move that was blocked by a judge. The Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority has recently been under increased scrutiny by local and federal officials. The county announced this year that it would seek a review of the agency’s financial and operational practices over delays in invoice processing and failure to pay county providers as scheduled. An audit earlier this year identified issues with the agency’s bookkeeping and accounting. Bass sits on the agency’s board – the first mayor in the city to do so – but has been absent from more than half of the meetings in the last three years, according to LAist. Congressman Robert Garcia described the move as “another attempt by Donald Trump and House Republicans to launch a witch hunt against Mayor Karen Bass and Los Angeles.” Chuck Schumer said Donald Trump was “[attempting] to destroy the integrity of our elections” by asking the supreme court to lift an order blocking USPS from implementing mail-in voting restrictions. The Senate Democratic leader said in a statement that the court should not “accelerate a case that so poisons our democracy”. Earlier Thursday, the Trump administration asked the court to step in to allow the USPS new system to regulate mail ballots to go into effect. “Americans are fed up with Trump, his failed war, and his rising costs. But instead of facing the voters, Trump is trying to make it harder for them to vote and hold him accountable for his horrific agenda.” In more redistricting news, Maryland’s supreme court has decided that a Democrat-backed congressional redistricting amendment can go before voters in the state in November. The ruling, a major victory for Democrats, comes after two lower courts first blocked it from appearing on ballots. The proposal could allow Democrats to create new congressional districts ahead of the 2028 election if voters approve it. Missouri’s supreme court has ruled that a Donald Trump-backed US House map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, preventing it from being used in the upcoming November election. The development was a blow to Republicans who were hoping the new congressional boundaries would help them keep a majority in the House in the midterms. Trump fumed over the ruling, describing it as “horrible, ridiculous, and unConstitutional” and arguing the election process was being “disturbed”. Catherine Hanaway, the state’s Republican attorney general, planned to appeal the decision to the supreme court. She argued it “thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis”. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries praised the ruling, calling it a “resounding victory for the people of the Show-Me State and a clear message to MAGA extremists trying to rig the midterm elections.” “The people are now empowered to decide what the congressional map should look like in November, not Donald Trump and corrupt Republicans,” Jeffries said. Energy, manufacturing, agriculture and transportation groups are appealing to Congress to take action to stop California clean car rules that it argues aim to “[limit] choice in vehicle and other engine purchasing decisions”. Dozens of groups, including the American Petroleum Institute, the US Chamber of Commerce and Agricultural Retailers Association, sent a letter to the leaders of the House and Senate asking for congressional intervention. The missive came one day after a federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from overturning a set of California vehicle pollution standards. “We strongly urge Congress to protect consumer choice by using its Congressional Review Act authority to disapprove these rule makings. Doing so will protect consumers, our economy, and our national security,” the authors wrote. Donald Trump announced an interim replacement for army secretary, Dan Driscoll, who suddenly resigned earlier this week amid reports of tension between him and defense secretary Pete Hegseth. The president said on Thursday that Adam Telle, who currently serves as the assistant secretary of the army office for civil works, will become the acting army secretary. “He is a Great Patriot, who is respected by all,” Trump said. Congressman Don Beyer, whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery, described Trump’s arch project as “illegal, gridlock-increasing [and] narcissistic” and criticized the administration for moving ahead with it. The representative pointed to a report from the the National Park Service – which supports the project – that found it would have adverse effects on multiple landmarks. “This project is not even close to being ready for prime time. The Administration has not won the legal battle over the proposal, which is plainly illegal without congressional authorization,” Beyer said in a statement. “The only study they have completed and released, from the National Park Service, confirms my admonition that the arch would be a massive, unnecessary disruption to iconic and historic sites across the region.” Excavation work on Donald Trump’s “Great Triumphal Arch” project in Washington is set to begin in the coming weeks, interior secretary Doug Burgum said on Thursday. The 250ft tall gilded structure will be built in between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. “This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World,” Burgum said. But critics say the arch will interfere with historic sightlines and that it has not received congressional authorization. Three veterans and an architectural historian filed a lawsuit over the project. “We believe that construction cannot and should not proceed apace, and we are prepared to inform the court that it needs to, at this juncture, needs to step in,” said Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with Public Citizen Litigation Group, who is representing the plaintiffs. As a federal judge is deciding whether to extend a ban on the USPS’s new mail-in voting restrictions, Donald Trump has asked the US supreme court to step in. The Justice ‌Department filed an emergency request seeking to have the court lift Judge Indira Talwani’s order that temporarily blocks the ⁠postal service from implementing the plan, which includes an online portal that would track millions of mail ballots. The new system to regulate mail ballots, which came about following an executive order by Trump, has drawn fierce criticism. A whistleblower told Congress that the requirements could result in scores of mail ballots never being sent. The Federal Emergency Management Agency appears to be downplaying $168 million in winter storm damage across New York City, Long Island, and Mid-Hudson region. In response to a query about New York Gov Kathy Hochul’s claim that federal authorities denied her request for disaster relief because of “political games,” FEMA said: “No new information was provided by New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island for FEMA to consider; they only repeated their requests for federal reimbursement of costs to plow snow.” “Winter weather is not new to the Northeast and neither is snow removal,” FEMA also said in its statement to The Guardian. “Federal disaster aid is not a backstop for routine state and local budgeting.” JD Vance’s comment about the US-Iran conflict that he “wouldn’t call it a war right now” has sparked criticism. Rep Ro Khanna, referring to this comment, said it was made “as if Americans can’t see what’s going on on their own phones, with their own eyes.” “It’s unbelievable gaslighting,” the California Democrat also said in a video posted to X. “This is war. You know who understands it’s a war? Donald Trump. He claims that we’re winning the war.” Former US pardon attorney Elizabeth Oyer on Thursday sued the department of justice and attorney general Todd Blanche, alleging that they “unlawfully” fired her last year after she said she rejected a recommendation to restore actor Mel Gibson’s gun rights. The Guardian’s Anna Betts reports that Oyer’s Washington DC federal court complaint maintains that in early 2025 she was asked to “disregard her duties and facilitate a political favor” for the embattled actor because of his “relationship with President Trump”. Oyer alleges that she was “asked to make it seem like an independent review had concluded that Mr Gibson, who was convicted of a domestic violence offense, should have his gun rights restored”. After Oyer declined, “she was fired by then deputy attorney general Todd Blanche”, her suit alleges. Read more of Betts’ reporting on Oyer’s lawsuit here. Moments before Vance’s presser ended, the vice president was asked an unexpected question: Did he and Trump know about Milo Yiannopoulos’s deportation? “So on Milo, I won’t speak for the president, but I found out, I think, like so many others found out.” “I found out about it publicly,” he also said of the rightwing provocateur’s deportation. “I’m not sure if the president knew about it beforehand, but I’m sure we can follow up with the president and get you an answer to that question.” Yiannopoulos recently broke his silence about being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Louisiana and deported to the United Kingdom, stating “for the first time I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified”. During an appearance on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Yiannopoulos said it was a “humiliating and disorientating” experience, as well as “physically degrading” and “frightening”. Yiannopoulos also said he was “ashamed” of his prior support for Trump and the mass deportation agenda. “I wouldn’t call it a war right now,” Vance said of the ongoing US-Iran conflict. “There is no active shooting.” “I recognize there is there have been places where this is flared up [but] major combat operations again, major combat operations lasted for about six weeks and since then, we destroyed, of course, their nuclear facilities…” JD Vance downplayed the disconnect between widespread opposition to data centers and Trump’s artificial intelligence fervor. Asked if a Democrat-held Congress would disadvantage US AI development, Vance agreed. He said there’s a “very good chance” that the US could be bested by China in the AI race if Democrats held Congress. “On the data center question, you asked how do how do you split the difference, or how do you bridge the gap?” Vance said. “The simple answer is the way that you bridge the gap is by following the president of the United States.” Vance said a lot of data center opposition – which is increasingly a bipartisan sentiment – stemmed from people worrying their neighborhood would get worse, that their power bills would go up. Vance said that Trump has pushed for ratepayer protection and insisted that data centers must return power back into the grid. “The way to bridge that gap is for people to do what the president United States has enabled. He’s made it easier to build a nuclear power plant, or any other power plant, next to a data center. He’s made it easier for people to put power back into the grid as opposed to take it out.” The vice president rebuffed Iran’s claims that US strikes hit a wedding party, saying that country’s state-run media has not been a “very good scribe” about covering the conflict. “I’m extremely skeptical of this. What I can say with 100% confidence is that unlike [Iran], the United States never targets civilians in combat. We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen,” Vance said in a response to a question about Iran’s claim. “But in this particular case, I don’t think that we have any information one way or the other. We’re investigating because obviously we care.” “We want to know, and if we do make mistakes – again, this is a big difference between us and Iran – when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them. “So we’re investigating it very quickly.” Vance also described Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – whose leadership of the military has come under immense scrutiny – as a “very good friend of mine.” And, Vance said, “I think he’s an amazing secretary of war. And, you know, fundamentally where I look, there are a lot of issues where I agree with Pete on the issue. Where I’m in the most strident agreement with Pete is that we needed to have a culture shift at the Department of War.” “What Pete came in wanting to do was revive the warrior spirit in the United States of America,” Vance said.
